1:
The siege is dated to the day. Gill notes the narrative agrees with Jeremiah's throughout, and the dating interests the rest. Ellicott points to the matching precision later in the chapter and Ezekiel's agreement, and notes these days were kept as fasts in the exile; the word rendered forts occurs only in Ezekiel, means some siege work nobody can specify, and comes out as wall in the Greek, palisade in the Syriac. Delitzsch reckons the siege at eighteen months, which shows what the fortifications must have been. Both record the interruption when Hophra's approach drew the besiegers off, Delitzsch judging they repulsed him without a battle, Clarke that Nebuchadnezzar routed the Egyptians and came back to invest the city closely. Wesley keeps to the works, raised to shut out provisions and to shoot from. Henry reads the encircling as theology: Jerusalem was once compassed with God's favour as with a shield, and now its defence had departed.

The famine is the next stage. Ellicott insists the scarcity was not first felt that day but had reached a climax at which defence became impossible, and recalls that here as at Samaria parents ate their children. Delitzsch refuses Seb. Schmidt's explanation that the hunger is recorded because it made resistance impossible, making it a proof of the prophetic word instead; he also finds a copyist's oversight, the words naming the fourth month having fallen out before the day. Ellicott supplies the same from Jeremiah, reporting a Syriac text that reads the fifth month and may be original. On the people of the land both part from Thenius, who as usual insists the militia are meant: Ellicott answers that the militia are the next verse's men of war, Wesley that these are the commons, not the great men. Henry hears retribution, a city punished for its fulness of bread and feeding itself without fear.

Then the wall breaks and the king runs. Ellicott has battering-rams like those in Assyrian sculptures and puts the entry on the north, in the Lower City, the generals next assaulting the middle gate that divides upper from lower; he observes that the Hebrew wants a verb and implies an unnamed king, so the parallels recommend reading that Zedekiah fled with the men of war; and he sites the gate between the two walls in the glen between Ophel and Zion, the double wall protecting Siloam. Delitzsch says the flight was discovered at once because the besiegers lay all round, as Ezekiel had foreseen. Ellicott adds that the plain is the Arabah, near Jericho twelve miles wide, its farther side the plains of Moab. Henry turns it to a sentence: those who think to escape God's judgments deceive themselves as much as those who brave them.

Riblah supplies the end. Ellicott notes Nebuchadnezzar was absent from the storm, awaiting the result at headquarters, where he tried Zedekiah as a rebel against his liege lord, the broken oath pressed hardest; Delitzsch has him open the siege in person, then hand it to his generals and withdraw to direct the campaign, and notes that Jeremiah puts the judgments in the plural where this text has the singular. Wesley explains the station practically, a place from which to supply the besiegers and watch Chaldea. On the sentence Ellicott observes that Jeremiah's verbs are singular, so the acts fall to Nebuchadnezzar, though the blinding need not have been his own hand, whoever acts through another acting himself; he calls blinding a Babylonian punishment and reads the fetters as a double brass, manacles and shackles. Wesley finds in the killing of the sons a declaration that the kingdom was over, and sets beside it the two predictions that seemed to contradict, that the king should go to Babylon yet never see it, which the false prophet of the same name could not reconcile and so called both false. Clarke notes the same pair fulfilled.
8:
The day of the burning is the first dispute. Ellicott calls the seventh an error for the tenth, one numeral letter mistaken for another, and reports a Syriac and Arabic ninth, which Thenius explains by the memorial fasts beginning on that evening. Gill flags the same gap between this text and Jeremiah's. Clarke dissolves it by chronology: Nebuzaradan entered on the seventh, spent two days provisioning, and fired the buildings on the tenth; Ellicott reads the name as a transcript of a Babylonian one meaning Nebo gave seed, and captain of the guard as strictly chief of executioners, commander of the royal bodyguard; Henry and Wesley both take the month between the capture and the burning for a space given to repent, and taken in vain.

The burning itself draws the longest reflection from Henry. That the holy and beautiful house should burn he finds strange, prepared for by David and built by Solomon at vast expense, yet not fire-proof against God's judgments; a people who trusted it for protection found it a refuge of lies. He puts its standing at some four hundred and twenty years and guesses the ark perished with it, since nothing more is heard of it in the second temple. Wesley dismisses the apocryphal story that Jeremiah hid the ark in a cave on Nebo, the prophet being then a close prisoner; both note the second temple burned on the same month and day. Ellicott corrects the English instead: every great man's house should be every great house, the common houses being spared for the poor left behind. Henry says sin unwalls a people, and these walls waited till Nehemiah. Wesley counts the deportation at eight hundred and thirty-two, and observes that the rich went prisoners abroad while the poor had liberty at home.

The brass comes next. Delitzsch explains the breaking up: the colossal pieces could hardly be moved whole. Henry reads a sign cancelled: Jachin and Boaz stood for the strength and stability of God's house, so when the thing signified was sinned away the signs had no business standing; and since Ahaz had already cut the borders from the bases, the brass was justly handed over. The loss of the ministering vessels, he adds, ended the ministration: those who would have many altars shall now have none. Ellicott turns technical: Jeremiah ceases to run parallel from this verse, brass should probably be copper throughout, without weight is a hyperbole much like the Assyrian boast of spoils without number, and the capital's three cubits is a transcription error for five. Gill reports Benjamin of Tudela's claim that the pillars stand in a church at Rome with Solomon's name engraved, sweating every ninth of Ab, and refuses it, since this verse says they were broken in pieces.

The officers close the account. Clarke, Gill and Ellicott agree the second priest is the sagan or deputy who served when the high priest was disabled, Gill adding the custom of appointing one seven days before the day of atonement. On Seraiah they part: Ellicott makes him Ezra's grandfather or great-grandfather, Henry his father. Ellicott takes the door-keepers for chief warders of the principal entrances, the whole temple leadership removed together. The five men divide the versions: Ellicott records five in the Greek, Syriac and Vulgate, fifty in the Targum, seven in Jeremiah and the Arabic, blaming a partly obliterated numeral, while Clarke guesses Jeremiah counted in the officer over the men of war and the scribe of the host. Delitzsch places them in the king's immediate circle and notices Jeremiah's past tense, marking the commander's office as ended with the city. Ellicott takes the threescore for the remnant of the citadel garrison, noting another view that they were ringleaders of the defence; Clarke has Nebuchadnezzar discover that they counselled the revolt, while Henry suspects divine justice saw in them the ringleaders of the idolatry.
22:
Gedaliah is defended by nearly all. Ellicott traces him to Ahikam, the prince who saved Jeremiah from popular fury, notes that Nebuzaradan committed the prophet to the son's care, and argues from his later conduct that he was no traitor, as some have misnamed him, but a disciple of Jeremiah urging the remnant to submit. Henry calls him one of themselves who would make the best of the bad, suspects he had gone over to the Chaldeans on Jeremiah's advice, and thinks him likelier to bless the people than many of their kings, having the prophet for a privy council. Clarke alone deflates the office: no regal dignity, but an overseer appointed to regulate husbandmen, which is how Gill reads it too. On Mizpah they divide, Ellicott noting its ancient sanctuary might serve in some sort for the ruined temple, Clarke reporting it east of Jordan while admitting several places bore the name.

Then the governor is killed. Ellicott dates it two months after the fall, at a friendly meal in Gedaliah's own house, perhaps, as Josephus has it, when the party was overcome with wine; he finds the motive in the assassin's royal blood and a claim he thought better than Gedaliah's, with the Ammonite king behind him. Delitzsch has him arrive with ten men and cut down the Jews and Chaldaeans about the governor as well, noting that Johanan's warning had been given and disbelieved. Clarke supplies the sequel: fourscore more killed as they came with offerings, prisoners taken including king's daughters, Johanan's pursuit, the prisoners turning on their captor, the murderer escaping with eight. Wesley puts it down to envy at seeing so mean a person advanced into their place. Henry calls him a degenerate branch of the house of David, no better enemy to their peace than Nebuchadnezzar.

The flight follows, and Henry thinks it the real end. They were still in their own good land and forsook it; had the innocent remonstrated that the murder was one man's act, those who suffered by it would probably not have been punished for it, so the full end came by their own folly and against the prophet's counsel. Delitzsch says only that they went for fear of the Chaldees, much fuller accounts surviving in Jeremiah. Ellicott notes they took Jeremiah with them and that this verse gives only the end of a story told elsewhere; Gill adds Baruch and the king's daughters to the company. Wesley guesses what became of them: mixed by degrees with the Egyptians and heard of no more as Israelites.

A last gleam closes it. Ellicott makes the thirty-seven years put Jehoiachin at fifty-five, prefers Jeremiah's twenty-fifth day to this text's twenty-seventh, and renders the king's name as man of Merodach, noting he was later murdered by his brother-in-law. Delitzsch blames similar letters, glosses lifting up the head as release and promotion together, an act of grace at a reign's beginning. Ellicott reads the precedence over the other captive kings as a higher chair of state in the royal hall, recalling Cyrus keeping Croesus at court. Clarke has the released king living in regal style with a court of his own in Babylon, and supposes he fell with his protector when that king was killed in a conspiracy two years later. Delitzsch refuses that inference, since the favour might have been continued by a successor; Ellicott says the writer dwells with pleasure on this faint gleam amid the darkness, a foreshadowing of the pity later shown the captive people. Henry reports a Jewish tradition that the Babylonian had himself been imprisoned by his father and there made friends with Jehoiachin, and dates the kindness to the midnight of the captivity, thirty-six of the seventy years gone. He and Wesley end on the same sentence: let none say they shall never see good again because they have long seen little but evil.
